Wondering why you should care about Chinese car license plates as a Mandarin learner?
If you don’t know what Chinese license plates look like, this may not immediately strike you as the most thrilling topic.
If you have been out on the Chinese roads and sufficiently attentive, however, you may have noticed that license plates , 车牌 (chēpái), in China actually pack a lot of information!
Chinese license plates use a unique system of color, character, and number combinations to denote all the key information about a vehicle.

By familiarising with this system, you can get surprising amounts of insight into not just any given vehicle and its owner – but also China’s geography, road traffic policies, and even cultural beliefs, at large.
This blog post is your guide to everything about Chinese license plates: from how to interpret the meanings of their different components and colors, to the steps for getting one yourself.
And, as a bonus, also an overview of some China-specific license plate regulations, restrictions, and cultural values you may not have been aware of!
What Does a Standard Chinese License Plate Look Like?

What do the Different Colors of Chinese License Plates Mean?
Besides the license plates’ numbers and characters, you should also pay attention to their color.
In China, the color of license plates indicates the type of vehicle or its registration status.
Blue, yellow, and green are the three most common colors, but you may occasionally also come across others, such as black and white.
In this section, we will explain what each of these colors mean.
*   Formats vary, but will include some letters, characters, or symbols to denote their function.
For example, police vehicles will include a 警 (j ǐ ng) character, while military vehicles “WJ”.
Number-Based driving bans, 限号 (xiàn hào) in Mandarin, is the most common license plate restriction affecting all privately-owned vehicles in major cities.

Even-Odd Day Restrictions, 单双号限行 (dān shuāng hào xiàn xíng), is another type of license plate restriction in China which will be implemented under special circumstances, for example periods of severe air pollution of major international events, such as the Olympics or G20 Summit.
Non-local Car Driving Bans, 外地车限行 (wài dì chē xiàn xíng), is another type of license plate restriction in China which is designed to prioritize local residents in crowded cities.
Other cities, most famously Shanghai, instead use an auction system where license plates are awarded to the highest bidder.
In May 2023, a new-energy-vehicle magazine reported that at the monthly Shanghai auction, the lowest winning price of a license plate was RMB 92,400, and the average price of RMB 92,547.

To give you some sense of scale, the 2025 BYD Seagull electric vehicle is available starting at just about half of that price (56,800 yuan)… so when people complain that license plates are more expensive than cars in Shanghai, they do mean it literally.
Other cities have implemented a hybrid system whereby they allocate license plates through a combination of the two systems above.
When this system was first pioneered in Guangzhou in 2012, the split was 50% through lotteries, 40% through auctions, and 10% reserved for new-energy vehicles.
Buy a car (must have a residence permit in that city) and obtain a formal purchase invoice, which will be a key document to prove the source of the vehicle.
Pay vehicle purchase compulsory insurances.
Visit the local Department of Motor Vehicles (车辆管理所) to register your vehicle.
In addition to showing your vehicle purchase invoice, tax certificate, insurance details, and personal ID, you may have to fill out some additional forms and pass a vehicle inspection.
After passing, you will receive a vehicle registration certificate.
Apply for a license plate.
Once you have received your vehicle registration certificate, you can apply for a license plate.
The procedures for this will vary depend on whether your city has a license plate quota system implemented, and if so, whether it is a lottery or auction systems.
**Beijing**: Beijing Vehicle Management Office, No. 18 South Fourth Ring East Road, Chaoyang District.
**Guangzhou**: Guangzhou Municipal Public Security Bureau Vehicle Administration Office of the Traffic Police Squad, No. 1732 Huaguan Road, Tianhe District.
**Shanghai**: No. 1 Branch of Vehicle Administrative Office, No. 2999 West Huaxia Road, Pudong New District.

**Shenzhen**: Shenzhen Public Security Bureau Traffic Police Bureau Vehicle Management Office, Xinyi Auto City, Henggang Town, Longgang District, Shenzhen Public Security Bureau Traffic Police Bureau.
Note that some of these offices may require you to make an appointment, while others allow you to just show up.
Make sure to check this beforehand.
As we have covered before, numbers hold a very special significance in Chinese culture.
The numbers on car license plates are no exception!

Just like with phone numbers, house numbers, and Wi-Fi passwords, certain numbers on license plates in China are favored (or avoided) based on their phonetic resemblance to auspicious or inauspicious words in Mandarin.
*   **8 (****八****bā)**: Sounds like “发” (fā), meaning to get rich.
*   **6 (****六****liù)**: Sounds like “流” (liú), meaning smooth or successful.
*   **9 (****九****ji****ǔ****)**: Sounds like “久” (ji ǔ), meaning long-lasting or eternal.
*   **4 (****四****sì)**: Sounds like “死” (s ǐ, death).

The cultural significance of these lucky and unlucky numbers is so strong in China that people sometimes are willing to pay enormous premiums for a plate with more sixes, eights, and nines. (And equally, will avoid those with fours at all costs).
As a result, auspicious number plates have become a status symbol.

In Hong Kong for example, the numbers 18 and 9 sold for $2.1 million (USD) and $1.7 million respectively – and a plate with “28” (which sounds similar to the words for “easy” and “to prosper” in Cantonese), set the record for the highest price ever paid for a license plate at a staggering $2.3 million!
So much more to a license plate than you thought, right?

Even if you are not a car enthusiast, or looking to buy a car in China at the moment, we hope this blog has given you some interesting insight into the uniquely complicated world of Chinese license plates.

Hopefully next time you’re walking down a street in China, gazing out the window of your DiDi, or at the C-drama on your laptop screen, you will be paying a little extra attention to the vehicles passing by!
Why not test yourself, and maybe even your friends, on how much information you can gather about them based on the characters, numbers, and colors of their license plates?
After all, fun and effective language learning is all about finding the opportunities to learn through the everyday!
### Since Chinese has no alphabet, what is used on the license plates in China?
Chinese license plates use a combination of Chinese characters, Latin alphabet letters, and numbers.
A standard Chinese license plate consists of one Chinese character, followed by a Latin alphabet letter, and then a series of five numbers or letters, such as 京 A·12345.
### What does the first character on Chinese licence plates mean?
The first character on a standard Chinese license plate represents the province or municipality where the vehicle is registered, for example 京 for Beijing, 沪 for Shanghai, and 粤 for Guangzhou.
### What color are Chinese license plates?
The three most common colors of license plates in China is blue for small private vehicles, yellow for large and commercial vehicles, and green for new energy vehicles.
You may occasionally also see other colors for special-use vehicles, such as black for foreign or diplomatic vehicles, or white for military, police, or official use.
### How do I get a Chinese license plate?
As a foreigner, you need to meet certain eligibility criteria to buy a car and apply for a license plate in China, such as having a valid residence permit and Chinese driving license.
After this, the procedures vary regionally, depending for example on whether your city has a lottery or auction-based license plate quota system in place.
